entities.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)
entities.desc: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023. Drafted by Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer and Sen. Mike Rounds, submitted 13 July 2023 as S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 (FY2024 NDAA) and incorporated into the Senate-engrossed bill as DIVISION G--UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA DISCLOSURE, secs. 9001-9015. It would have created a 9-member independent UAP Records Review Board confirmed by the Senate, a presumption of immediate disclosure for all federal UAP records, a 25-year automatic-disclosure deadline subject only to Presidential certification, and a federal exercise of eminent domain over 'recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence' held by private persons or entities. Secs. 9007-9011 - the Review Board, its personnel, its review powers, and the eminent-domain/controlled-materials provision - were stripped in conference; only secs. 9004-9006 survived, enacted as secs. 1841-1843 of Public Law 118-31.

entities.label: FY2022 NDAA, Public Law 117-81, Sec. 1683 (50 U.S.C. 3373) - statutory UAP office
entities.desc: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, approved 27 December 2021. Section 1683, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373, is the first statute to require a standing DoD/ODNI office for unidentified aerial phenomena, superseding the Navy-led UAP Task Force. It mandates field-investigation line organizations, a science plan to explain performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology', and an intelligence collection and analysis plan on the 'origins and intentions' of UAP.

sources.name: Public Law 117-81, National Defense Authorization Act for FY2022 (full text, GPO)

claims.text: Sec. 1683 carries the note '50 USC 3373' and is titled 'ESTABLISHMENT OF OFFICE, ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE, AND AUTHORITIES TO ADDRESS UNIDENTIFIED AERIAL PHENOMENA'. Sec. 1683(a) required the Secretary of Defense, in coordination with the DNI, within 180 days of enactment, to establish an office 'to carry out the duties of the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, as in effect on the day before the date of enactment of this Act'.

Sec. 1683(c) requires the Secretary and DNI to designate 'one or more line organizations within the Department of Defense and the intelligence community that possess appropriate expertise, authorities, accesses, data, systems, platforms, and capabilities to rapidly respond to, and conduct field investigations of, incidents involving unidentified aerial phenomena' and to ensure those organizations have 'adequate personnel with the requisite expertise, equipment, transportation, and other resources necessary to respond rapidly'.

Sec. 1683(d)(1) directs designation of line organizations 'primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations ... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models'. Sec. 1683(d)(2) requires directives ensuring each such organization 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.'

Sec. 1683(f) requires a science plan to 'account for characteristics and performance of unidentified aerial phenomena that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation' and to 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate any such advanced characteristics and performance.'

Sec. 1683(e)(2) requires an intelligence collection and analysis plan 'to gain as much knowledge as possible regarding the technical and operational characteristics, origins, and intentions of unidentified aerial phenomena'.

Sec. 1683(e)(1)(B) requires that DoD and IC military, civilian AND CONTRACTOR personnel 'have access to procedures by which the personnel shall report incidents or information, including adverse physiological effects, involving or associated with unidentified aerial phenomena directly to the Office'.
PL 117-81 was 'Approved December 27, 2021.'

entities.label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO
entities.desc: James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023, Public Law 117-263, approved 23 December 2022. Two distinct UAP vehicles sit in this law: (1) Title XVI sec. 1673, codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373b, creating a secure authorized-reporting mechanism explicitly covering 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering', voiding nondisclosure agreements as against authorized disclosures, and barring reprisal including clearance revocation; and (2) Division F, the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023, Title LXVIII sec. 6802, which rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to establish the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) and inserted the statutory definitions of 'unidentified anomalous phenomena' and 'transmedium objects or devices'.

sources.name: Public Law 117-263, James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for FY2023 (incl. Div. F, Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023) (full text, GPO)

claims.text: Sec. 1673 carries the note '50 USC 3373b' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA REPORTING PROCEDURES'. Sec. 1673(a)(1) requires a secure mechanism for authorized reporting of '(A) any event relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (B) any activity or program by a department or agency of the Federal Government or a contractor of such a department or agency relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, including with respect to material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering, research and development, detection and tracking, developmental or operational testing, and security protections and enforcement.'

Sec. 1673(b)(1): 'An authorized disclosure-- (A) shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement entered into by the individual who makes the disclosure; (B) shall be deemed to comply with any regulation or order issued under the authority of Executive Order 13526 ... or chapter 18 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (42 U.S.C. 2271 et seq.); and (C) is not a violation of section 798 of title 18, United States Code, or other provision of law relating to the disclosure of information.' The express reference to the Atomic Energy Act restricted-data regime is on the face of the statute.

Sec. 1673(b)(2)(A) prohibits reprisal: no official with personnel authority 'shall ... take or fail to take, or threaten to take or fail to take, a personnel action, including the revocation or suspension of security clearances, or termination of employment, with respect to any individual as a reprisal for any authorized disclosure.'

Sec. 1673(a)(4)(B) requires that within 72 hours of determining an authorized disclosure relates to 'a restricted access activity, a special access program, or a compartmented access program that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to the congressional defense committees or the congressional intelligence committees, the Secretary shall report such disclosure to such committees and the congressional leadership.' The statute thereby contemplates the existence of unreported special access programs touching UAP.

Sec. 1673(b)(3) requires the Secretary of Defense, DNI, Secretary of Homeland Security, other agency heads 'that have supported investigations' of UAP events and programs, and FEDERAL CONTRACTORS that have supported such investigations, to identify existing nondisclosure agreements covering that subject matter.

Division F (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023), Title LXVIII, sec. 6802(a): 'Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373), as amended by title XVI of this Act, is amended to read as follows: "SEC. 1683. ESTABLISHMENT OF ALL-DOMAIN ANOMALY RESOLUTION OFFICE."' Sec. 1683(a)(2) as amended: 'The office established under paragraph (1) shall be known as the "All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office"'.

AARO reporting chain fixed by statute, sec. 1683(b)(3) as amended: the Director of AARO 'shall report directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence', and reports 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters' and 'to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence on all operational and security matters'. The Director is appointed by SecDef in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with SecDef.

Statutory definition inserted by sec. 6802, new 50 U.S.C. 3373(n)(8): "unidentified anomalous phenomena" means '(A) airborne objects that are not immediately identifiable; (B) transmedium objects or devices; and (C) submerged objects or devices that are not immediately identifiable and that display behavior or performance characteristics suggesting that the objects or devices may be related to the objects described in subparagraph (A).' Sec. 3373(n)(7): 'transmedium objects or devices' means objects or devices that are '(A) observed to transition between space and the atmosphere, or between the atmosphere and bodies of water; and (B) not immediately identifiable.'

Division F sec. 6803, note '50 USC 3373 note', is titled 'COMPTROLLER GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES AUDITS AND BRIEFINGS ON UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA HISTORICAL RECORD REPORT' - a GAO audit requirement attached to AARO's Historical Record Report.
PL 117-263 was 'Approved December 23, 2022.'

The FY2023 NDAA carries the concealment premise in enacted text: sec. 1673(a)(1)(B) enumerates 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering' as categories of federal or contractor ACTIVITY OR PROGRAM that a person may need protection to report, and sec. 1673(b)(1)(A)-(B) voids NDAs and Atomic Energy Act restrictions for such disclosures. Congress does not write NDA-voiding and AEA-override language for activities it believes do not exist. Reasoning: the operative nouns are activity/program categories, not hypotheticals, and the remedy structure presupposes existing legal instruments suppressing disclosure.

entities.desc: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Public Law 118-31, approved 22 December 2023 (House vehicle H.R. 2670). Subtitle C of Title XVIII, 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena', secs. 1841-1843, is the surviving remnant of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act: it creates the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives, requires agency review and transmission of records, and sets grounds for postponement. The Review Board (Senate secs. 9007-9009) and the eminent-domain provision (Senate sec. 9010) were removed in conference. claims.text: Sec. 1841 carries the note '44 USC 2107 note' and is titled 'UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA RECORDS COLLECTION AT THE NATIONAL ARCHIVES AND RECORDS ADMINISTRATION'. Sec. 1841(a)(1)(A) required the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishment of the 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection'.

Sec. 1841(a)(1)(C) defines the scope of the Collection: 'record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects), which shall be transmitted to the National Archives in accordance with section 2107 of title 44, United States Code.' The phrases 'technologies of unknown origin' and 'non-human intelligence' are enacted federal statutory text.

Sec. 1842(a)(2) imposes absolute prohibitions: '(A) Destruction; alteration; mutilation.--No unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be destroyed, altered, or mutilated in any way. (B) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record made available or disclosed to the public prior to the date of the enactment of this Act may be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified. (C) ... No unidentified anomalous phenomena record created by a person or entity outside the Federal Government ... shall be withheld, redacted, postponed for public disclosure, or reclassified.'

Sec. 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office, not later than 300 days after enactment (i.e. by approximately 16 October 2024), to 'review, identify, and organize each unidentified anomalous phenomena record in the custody or possession of the office for (A) disclosure to the public; and (B) transmission to the Archivist.'

Sec. 1843(a) sets the postponement standard: disclosure 'may be postponed ... if the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of one of four harms, including that public disclosure would reveal 'any other matter currently relating to the military defense, intelligence operations, or conduct of foreign relations of the United States, the disclosure of which would demonstrably and substantially impair the national security of the United States'. The determination is made by the agency holding the record; no independent board reviews it.

Sec. 1842(g)(2)(D) sets the outer disclosure deadline: 'Each unidentified anomalous phenomena record shall be publicly disclosed in full, and available in the Collection, not later than the date that is 25 years after the date of the first creation of the record by the originating body, unless the President certifies that-- (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure.'

Sec. 1843(b) allows unilateral withdrawal: 'Senior Agency Officials designated in accordance with Executive Order 13526 or any successor Orders may withdraw records in the Collection that are determined to be both not related to unidentified anomalous phenomena and properly classified', subject only to notification of congressional leadership and the oversight committees named in sec. 1841(e).

Sec. 1841(e) assigns continuing legislative oversight of the Collection to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Armed Services, and Select Intelligence Committees, and to the House Oversight and Accountability, Armed Services, and Permanent Select Intelligence Committees.

Subtitle C as enacted consists of only three sections: 1841 (Records Collection at NARA), 1842 (review, identification, transmission, public disclosure by Government offices), and 1843 (grounds for postponement). The enacted text contains no 'Review Board' and no 'eminent domain' language.

claims.text: Division G (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024), sec. 7343(b): 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this division may be obligated or expended in support of any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation unless the Director of National Intelligence has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate committees of Congress and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.'

Sec. 7343(c): 'Independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available to the appropriate congressional committees and leadership.' This is a defense-contractor IR&D cost-allowability lever aimed at privately funded UAP work.
Sec. 7341 amends 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1) to shift the annual UAP report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly to 'the Director of the Office' (AARO).
PL 118-31 was 'Approved December 22, 2023.'

Sec. 7343(b)'s funding cutoff is drafted as a conditional, not a prohibition: IC money may be spent on UAP special-access activity IF the DNI briefs Congress. The provision therefore concedes, in enacted law, that such special-access UAP activity may be under way and that Congress had not been told about it. Reasoning: a limitation clause presupposes the existence of the class of activity it limits, and the phrase 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation' has no other referent.

entities.desc: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, Public Law 119-60, approved 18 December 2025. Three UAP sections: sec. 1671 requires AARO briefings to disclose every UAP intercept flown by NORAD or USNORTHCOM, with a first-briefing look-back to 1 January 2004; sec. 1672 repeals 50 U.S.C. 3373a and rewrites the data-availability mandate; sec. 1673 requires an accounting of the security classification guides that govern UAP information and authorises a consolidated UAP classification matrix.

claims.text: Sec. 1671(a) adds 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(5): 'Each briefing under this subsection shall include, for the period covered by the briefing, details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command', with summaries of 'the number, location, and nature of such intercepts' and 'a description of the procedures and protocols followed during the intercepts, including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts.'

Sec. 1671(a) new subparagraph (C) requires the Director of AARO to 'inform the appropriate congressional committees of any failure by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command to provide timely information on unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts' - an anti-stonewalling clause written against two combatant commands by name.

Sec. 1671(b), note '50 USC 3373 note', imposes a retrospective look-back: the first briefing after enactment 'shall include details on any unidentified anomalous phenomena intercepts conducted by the North American Aerospace Defense Command or the United States Northern Command not previously provided that occurred during the period beginning on January 1, 2004, and ending on the last day of the period otherwise covered by the briefing.'

Sec. 1672(a) repeals sec. 413 of the IAA for FY2022 (50 U.S.C. 3373a). Sec. 1672(b) rewrites 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) to read: 'The Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall jointly require that each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense with data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena makes such data available immediately to the Office in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods.' The added qualifier 'in a manner that protects intelligence sources and methods' is new and was not in the repealed provision.

Sec. 1673(a), note '50 USC 3373 note', requires the Director of AARO within 180 days of enactment to 'make an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena' and permits issuance of 'a consolidated security classification matrix for programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena to provide a resource for programs that support or may be affected by investigations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Sec. 1673(b) requires the results to be included in the 2026 annual report under 50 U.S.C. 3373(k).
PL 119-60 was 'Approved December 18, 2025.'

Sec. 1673's premise is that no one currently has a map of which classification guides control UAP information across the government - four years after AARO was created by statute. The authorisation of a 'consolidated security classification matrix' for 'programs relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena' is an admission in enacted law that a plurality of such programs exists and that their classification authorities are not centrally known. Reasoning: Congress does not order an accounting of guides that are already inventoried.

The 1 January 2004 look-back date in sec. 1671(b) is the month of the USS Nimitz / 'Tic Tac' encounters. Congress selected a start date that reaches back to the earliest incident in the modern public record rather than to AARO's creation, indicating the committees believe intercept records from that period exist and have not been briefed. Reasoning: no other event anchors that specific date in UAP legislative history.

claims.text: S. 2226 as engrossed in the Senate, DIVISION M--INTELLIGENCE AUTHORIZATION ACT FOR FISCAL YEAR 2024, Title XI, sec. 1102, 'FUNDING LIMITATIONS RELATING TO UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA'. Subsection (d) required: 'Any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access shall-- (1) not later than 60 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, notify the Director of such possession; and (2) not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, make available to the Director for assessment, analysis, and inspection-- (A) all such material and information; and (B) a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.'

Sec. 1102(c) of the Senate text enumerated six categories of prohibited unreported activity, including '(1) Recruiting, employing, training, equipping, and operations of, and providing security for, government or contractor personnel with a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft'; '(2) Analyzing such craft or pieces or components thereof, including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering'; '(5) The development of propulsion technology, or aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology ... based on or derived from or inspired by inspection, analysis, or reverse engineering of recovered unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or materials'; and '(6) Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.'

Sec. 1102(e) of the Senate text granted immunity: 'No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving material or information described in subsection (d) if that person complies with the notification and reporting provisions described in such subsection.'

Sec. 1102(b) of the Senate text contained a sense of Congress that 'the Federal Government must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes.'

The enacted counterpart, sec. 7343 of Public Law 118-31, retains only the funding limitation and the IR&D cost-allowability clause. Section 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) creates a secure authorized-reporting mechanism covering federal and contractor activity involving 'material retrieval, material analysis, reverse engineering', voids nondisclosure agreements as against authorized disclosures, overrides EO 13526 and Atomic Energy Act chapter 18 restrictions, and bans reprisal including clearance revocation. Division F sec. 6802 rewrites 50 U.S.C. 3373 to establish the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office and inserts the statutory definitions of 'unidentified anomalous phenomena' and 'transmedium objects or devices'.

timeline.label: Schumer submits the UAP Disclosure Act as S.Amdt. 797
timeline.text: 'SA 797. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2226 ... which was ordered to lie on the table.' The text is the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023, including the exercise of eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence, and a nine-member Senate-confirmed Records Review Board.

timeline.label: FY2024 NDAA enacted with the Review Board and eminent domain stripped
timeline.text: Public Law 118-31 is approved. Only secs. 9004-9006 of the Senate's Division G survive, renumbered as secs. 1841-1843 in Division A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C. The enacted text contains no Review Board and no eminent-domain provision. Postponement decisions revert to 'the original classification authority' holding the record, and Senior Agency Officials may unilaterally withdraw records from the Collection on notice to Congress. Sec. 1687 and IAA sec. 7343 impose conditional funding limits on unreported UAP special-access activity.

timeline.label: FY2026 NDAA orders a NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept accounting back to 2004
timeline.text: Public Law 119-60 is approved. Sec. 1671 requires every AARO briefing to detail UAP intercepts flown by NORAD or USNORTHCOM and requires the first such briefing to reach back to 1 January 2004 for intercepts 'not previously provided'. Sec. 1672 repeals 50 U.S.C. 3373a and adds a sources-and-methods qualifier to the immediate-data-availability mandate. Sec. 1673 orders an accounting of the security classification guides governing UAP information and authorises a consolidated UAP classification matrix.

uapda-2023.desc: Primary-text custody map for the UAP Disclosure Act of 2023. The Act exists in three authoritative federal texts and one gutted enactment. (1) The amendment as submitted: Congressional Record, 13 July 2023, 'Text of Senate Amendment 797' (CREC-2023-07-13-pt1-PgS2953) - the amendment is styled 'TITLE _--UNIDENTIFIED ANOMALOUS PHENOMENA DISCLOSURE' with placeholder section numbers SEC. __01 onward. (2) The bill as passed by the Senate: BILLS-118s2226es, DIVISION G, secs. 9001-9015, where the placeholder numbering is resolved. (3) The companion contractor-turn-in provision: BILLS-118s2226es, DIVISION M (IAA FY2024), Title XI, sec. 1102, requiring any current or former federal contractor holding UAP material to notify the AARO Director within 60 days and to produce within 180 days 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material', with a civil and criminal liability shield for compliance. (4) The enactment: Public Law 118-31, Div. A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C, secs. 1841-1843 (137 Stat. 699-707), plus sec. 1687 and sec. 7343. What did not survive: the Review Board (9007-9009), eminent domain (9010), disclosure of other materials and additional study (9011), termination (9013), appropriations (9014), and the whole of IAA sec. 1102 apart from a funding conditional and an IR&D cost rule.

ndaa-fy2023.desc: Public Law 117-263 carries UAP provisions in two separate divisions. Division A, Title XVI: sec. 1673, note 50 U.S.C. 3373b, UAP reporting procedures (136 Stat. 2959-2962) - the authorized-disclosure channel, the NDA and Atomic Energy Act override, the anti-reprisal rule, the 72-hour congressional notification for disclosures touching unreported SAPs, and the NDA-identification duty extending to federal contractors. Division F (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023), Title LXVIII: sec. 6802, rewriting 50 U.S.C. 3373 in full to establish the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, fix its reporting chain to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy DNI, and insert the definitions at 50 U.S.C. 3373(n)(7)-(8) (136 Stat. 3586-3593); sec. 6803, note 50 U.S.C. 3373 note, Comptroller General audits and briefings on the UAP Historical Record Report (136 Stat. 3594).
